back: We use the continuous with state verbs (attract, like, look, love) to emphasize that a situation is temporary or for a period around the present [1].
Verbs such as believe, consist of, doubt, and own are rarely used with the present continuous [1].
Simple: 'seem' (e.g., 'The app doesn't appear to work'). Continuous: 'take part' (e.g., 'She is currently appearing in a musical') [1].
The continuous can emphasize that we have recently started to think about something or are not sure about it [1].
When it means 'think carefully about', it is only used with the present continuous [1].
Verbs like agree, believe, conclude, know, and prefer are rarely used with the present continuous [1].
Verbs which perform the action they describe (e.g., suggest, request, apologise) [1].
We use the present simple with performatives in affirmative sentences (e.g., 'I suggest you park outside') [1].
We can use either the present simple or present continuous (e.g., 'I don't deny' or 'I'm not denying') [1].
Modals (would, must) make performatives more tentative or polite (e.g., 'We would advise you to arrive early') [1].
Simple: to have an opinion. Continuous: the mental process of considering something [1].
Simple: to have an opinion. Continuous: can indicate a temporary physical or mental feeling [1].
Simple: to have a particular appearance. Continuous: can be used for temporary appearance or the action of looking [1].
Acknowledge, admit, advise, beg, confess, congratulate, declare, deny, forbid, guarantee, etc [1].
Examples of performative verbs that typically take the present simple in affirmative sentences [1].
